implementation_notes: Jest's mock function API is configured as in JavaScript (mockReturnValue, mockImplementation, mockResolvedValue, mockRejectedValue, and the ...Once variants), and TypeScript keeps the collaborator's types in the picture: jest.mocked(source) returns a jest.Mocked<T>-typed value whose member functions keep their signatures, so a renamed or retyped method fails compilation instead of silently configuring nothing. jest.Mock<T> narrows individual mock functions, and the module must be imported from @jest/globals for the typed API. That typed configuration surface is what replaces a hand-written configuration interface.
pitfalls: jest.mocked() is a typing helper only: it performs no runtime conversion, so the object must already have mock functions where they are configured.
Casting with as jest.Mocked<T> (instead of jest.mocked) silences the compiler even for a partial double, which reintroduces the silent mis-configuration the typed API avoids.
Mocks are module-global per test file; without resetting them in beforeEach, typed or not, the configured answers leak between tests.

variants.name: Hand-written typed fake class
variants.idiom_name: class implementing the collaborator interface with settable response fields
variants.implementation_notes: A class declares implements Clock, so the compiler forces every member to exist, and the answers are constructor parameters or settable fields the test assigns; the double is then an ordinary object that works under any runner (vitest, node:test, Jest) and carries its own types, including when the collaborator's API uses generics or overloads that mock typing handles awkwardly. Prefer it when the double needs real behaviour (in-memory store, call log) or when the test suite must not depend on a mocking library's type definitions.
pitfalls: implements is erased at runtime, so the double is only checked while it is compiled against the interface; passing it through any/unknown discards the check.
Fields are mutable, so a fake shared by several tests must be re-created or re-configured; TypeScript will not warn about a stale configuration.
Overloads and generics must be modelled explicitly in the fake, which can make it noisier than the interface it implements.
